content: Sylvite is the naturally occurring mineral form of potassium chloride (KCl). It crystallizes in the isometric system, exhibiting a structure that is very similar to that of halite (NaCl), commonly known as rock salt. In fact, sylvite and halite are isomorphous, meaning they share the same crystal structure. Sylvite is typically colorless to white, but it can display shades of yellow or red due to the presence of inclusions. It has a salty taste with a distinct bitterness. Sylvite is one of the last evaporite minerals to precipitate from a solution, which means it forms only in extremely arid, saline environments. Its primary application is as a potassium fertilizer, making it an important resource in agriculture. Sylvite is found in numerous evaporite deposits around the world. In the United States, significant deposits occur in New Mexico, western Texas, and Utah. However, the largest known deposits globally are located in Saskatchewan, Canada. These vast deposits in Saskatchewan were formed through the evaporation of a Devonian seaway. Sylvite is recognized as the official mineral of Saskatchewan. The mineral was first described in 1832 at Mount Vesuvius near Naples, Italy. It was named in honor of the Dutch chemist François Sylvius de le Boe (1614–1672).
